title: Front-of-house areas: housekeeping, toys and shared devices
audience: Cleaners who keep dental front-of-house and non-clinical spaces clean.
learningOutcomes: Apply a housekeeping method that avoids raising dust or aerosols.
Clean toys and shared devices on a set schedule.
Keep clinical and general cleaning tools separate.

instruction.heading: Housekeeping surfaces are still surfaces
instruction.body: Floors, walls, curtains and reception furniture carry lower risk than the clinical contact surfaces, but the source requires them to remain clean and sanitary under the public health rules that apply in each state and territory. Dust, soil and transient organisms still collect on them, so they stay on a written schedule.

instruction.heading: Toys and shared objects
instruction.body: Toys in waiting areas act as objects that carry germs between people. Wiping their firm surfaces with detergent wipes suited to firm clinical surfaces, on the practice's schedule and after a busy period, reduces the organisms that move around. Follow the product's own directions, and do not use general household spray in its place.

instruction.heading: Keyboards and handsets
instruction.body: Keyboards in the operatory can harbour microbes, so they are shielded in the treatment areas and wiped down between appointments with a product the manufacturer permits. Outside the treatment areas, keyboards are wiped down regularly. Standard keyboards cannot be submerged, and repeated saturation damages them, so flat or sealed keyboards are preferred where the practice can use them. Telephone handsets, door handles and window sills belong on the weekly schedule.

instruction.heading: Dusting and mopping without spreading dust
instruction.body: Cleaning must not stir up dust or spray. Damp dusting, mops that trap dust, and vacuums fitted with filtered exhaust are preferred, and brooms are kept out of clinical spaces. Mops and cloths are rinsed once used and left to air dry before the next use, or single-use heads are chosen. Keep separate mops for clinical and general areas, which the Malaysian guideline also advises. Lunchroom crockery is never washed in hand basins or instrument basins, and food is never stored with dental materials, specimens or medicines.

procedure: Wipe the firm surfaces of waiting-room toys with the approved wipes on the practice schedule.
Wipe keyboards outside the treatment areas, and check that keyboards inside them are shielded.
Damp dust or use a dust-retaining mop. Do not sweep dry.
Keep one mop for clinical areas and another for general areas, and dry them after each use.
Keep lunchroom crockery out of hand basins and instrument basins.
Record the completed tasks on the weekly schedule.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner is asked to sweep the treatment room floor with a broom to save time.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the correct method for the treatment room?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not sweep in a clinical area. Use a damp or dust-retaining method, or a vacuum with filtered exhaust, and keep the clinical mop separate from the general mop.

workedExamples.situation: Waiting-room toys have been handled by a crowd of children during a busy weekend.
workedExamples.reasoning: Wipe the hard surfaces with the approved wipes as an extra to the scheduled clean, and record that the extra clean was done.

equipmentAndPpe: Detergent wipes suited to firm clinical surfaces
Dust-retaining mop and a vacuum with filtered exhaust
Separate, colour-coded mops for clinical and general areas

commonErrors.error: Using a broom where clinical work happens.
commonErrors.prevention: Use damp or dust-retaining methods instead.

commonErrors.error: Using the same mop in the operatory and the reception area.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep separate mops and dry them between uses.

commonErrors.error: Washing lunch dishes in the instrument basin.
commonErrors.prevention: Use a kitchen sink for crockery.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Detergent wipes are chemicals. Follow the label and the practice's list of approved products.
Waiting-room and reception cleaning is governed by public health rules set by each state and territory. The schedules in this lesson are general; check them for your local area.
The Malaysian and Australian sources set cleaning frequencies differently. This lesson does not set a frequency, and the practice schedule applies.
The source names Australian standards and state rules.

qualityStandard: Toys and hard surfaces are cleaned on the practice schedule.
Clinical and general mops are kept separate and are dry between uses.
documentationEvidence: Record of any extra cleaning after a busy period
summary: Housekeeping surfaces still need a written schedule and clean methods that avoid dust.
Toys and shared devices are wiped with approved wipes, and keyboards are protected in treatment areas.
Separate clinical and general mops, and keep crockery out of instrument basins.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which mop approach fits a dental practice?
options: One mop for the surgery and the reception area used together without rinsing.
Separate mops for clinical and general areas, cleaned and dried after use.
A mop left wet in the bucket between rooms and used again on the next room.
A broom swept through the operatory after each patient visit.

knowledgeChecks.question: A waiting-room toy has been handled by several children. What is the right step?
options: Give it to the next child, because a quick rinse is enough and it can go back on the shelf.
Wipe its firm surfaces with the approved wipes, on the schedule or after a busy period.
Rinse it in the crockery sink with the lunch dishes and then leave it to dry on the bench.
Give it to the next child straight after the last one and do not clean it.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why are traditional keyboards a concern for cleaning?
options: They are not waterproof, so repeated soaking damages them, and they can harbour organisms.
They are too small to wipe and each key must be lifted and cleaned by hand one at a time.
They are sterile after one wipe with a dry cloth and need no further cleaning at any time.
They do not need cleaning at all because they are always kept in a sealed bag at the desk.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which housekeeping method does the lesson prefer for dusting?
options: Dry dusting that sends dust into the air
Spraying the air to settle dust

sourceReferences: ADA Guidelines for Infection Control, 3rd ed. (Australian Dental Association, 2015), section B.6 (cleaning the environment: housekeeping surfaces, toys, keyboards, dusting and mop use); rights: user-held; reworded (no copying)
